ety.text: From Middle English vertu, virtue, borrowed from Anglo-Norman vertu, virtu, from Latin virtus (“manliness, bravery, worth, moral excellence”), from vir (“man”). Doublet of vertu. See virile. In this sense, displaced Old English cræft, whence Modern English craft.

senses.d: The idea of all that is good or excellent (in every sense of those terms) in a human being, collectively instantiated by a varying number of human traits known as "the virtues", the enumeration of which vary by the many virtue systems which have developed within different cultures, religions, and historical periods.
Accordance with moral principles; conformity of behaviour or thought with the strictures of morality; good moral conduct.
ex: Without virtue, there is no freedom.
“Virtue is an inner light that can prevail in every soul.”

senses.d: An attribute of a personality (a "personality trait") which predisposes a person to behaviors resulting in human goodness; an admirable quality.
A particular manifestation of moral excellence in a person.
Specifically, each of several qualities held to be particularly important, including the four cardinal virtues, the three theological virtues, or the seven virtues opposed to the seven deadly sins.
ex: Better to be excluded from society than to deny the virtue of citizenship.
The divine virtues of truth and equity are the only bands of friendship, the only supports of society.

senses.d: An inherently advantageous or excellent quality of something or someone; a favourable point, an advantage.
A creature embodying divine power, specifically one of the orders of heavenly beings, traditionally ranked above angels and archangels, and below seraphim and cherubim.
ex: Thrones, Dominations, Princedoms, Virtues, Powers; / For in possession such, not only of right, / I call ye, and declare ye now […].

senses.d: Specifically, moral conduct in sexual behaviour, especially of women; chastity.
The inherent power of a god, or other supernatural being.
The inherent power or efficacy of something (now only in phrases).

senses.d: In effect or essence, rather than in fact or reality; also, imitated, simulated.
ex: In fact a defeat on the battlefield, Tet was a virtual victory for the North, owing to its effect on public opinion.
Virtual addressing allows computer applications to believe that there is much more physical memory than actually exists.

senses.d: For practical purposes, though not technically; almost complete, very near.
ex: The angry peasants were a virtual army as they attacked the castle.

senses.d: Operating using a computer and/or online rather than physically present.
ex: a virtual assistant    a virtual personal trainer

senses.d: Simulated in a computer and/or online.
ex: virtual machine    virtual memory    virtual private network
The virtual world of his computer game allowed character interaction.

senses.d: Of a class member: capable of being overridden with a different implementation in a subclass.
Pertaining to a theoretical infinitesimal velocity in a mechanical system that does not violate the system's constraints; also, of other physical quantities: resulting from such a velocity.
ex: virtual displacement    virtual work

senses.d: Pertaining to a theoretical quality of something which would produce an observable effect if counteracting factors such as friction are disregarded; specifically, of a head of water: producing a certain pressure if friction, etc., is disregarded.

Chiefly in virtual focus: of a focus or point: from which light or other radiation apparently emanates; also, of an image: produced by light that appears to diverge from a point beyond the reflecting or refracting surface.
Pertaining to particles in temporary existence due to the Heisenberg uncertainty principle.
Of a quantum state: having an intermediate, short-lived, and unobservable nature.
Preceded by the: that which is imitated or simulated rather than existing in fact or reality; (countable) an instance of this.
That which is simulated in a computer and/or online; virtual reality; (countable) an instance of this; specifically (gambling), a computer simulation of a real-world sport such as horse racing.
A virtual (adjective sense 3.3) member function of a class.

First use in the computer context by David Gerrold in his 1972 book When HARLIE Was One.

senses.d: A submicroscopic, non-cellular structure that consists of a core of DNA or RNA surrounded by a protein coat, that requires a living host cell to replicate, and that sometimes causes disease in the host organism (such agents are often classed as nonliving infectious particles and less often as microorganisms).
ex: Viruses are the smallest and most simplified forms of life.
Bats host many high-profile viruses that can infect humans, including severe acute respiratory syndrome and Ebola.

senses.d: A species thereof.
ex: Meronym: virion (individual particle)
Some viruses, such as norovirus, cause sporadic outbreaks of gastroenteritis.

senses.d: An individual particle thereof: synonym of virion.
ex: Under electron microscopy, a few viruses were seen floating near the cells.

senses.d: A quantity of such infectious agents, considered en masse.
ex: Not much virus was detectable on a nucleic acid test; the viral load was very low.

senses.d: A disease caused by such an infectious agent; a viral illness.
ex: He's got a virus and had to stay home from school.

senses.d: Venom, as produced by a poisonous animal etc.
ex: Brazil, that inferno where every budding flower and every buzzing bluebottle fly bears a lascivious virus.

senses.d: A type of malware which can covertly transmit itself between computers via networks (especially the Internet) or removable storage such as disks by inserting its code into other executable files, often causing damage to systems and data; also computer virus.
ex: Wait a minute! Is this one of those virus emails?!

senses.d: Any type of malware.
Any malicious or dangerous entity that spreads from one place or person to another.
To send or infect an electronic device with a computer virus.
ex: I'm just going to virus anyone who tries cheating on this game.

ety.text: From Middle English virgine, from Old French virgine, from Latin virginem, accusative of virgō. Doublet of Virgo. Displaced native Old English fǣmne.

senses.d: A person who has never had sexual intercourse, or (uncommonly) an animal that has never mated.
ex: On the other hand, the daughter of a clergyman repeatedly performed fellatio instead of genital intercourse so that she could remain a virgin.
among students we studied , 60 % of the virgin females had had oral sex experience

senses.d: A person who has never engaged in any sexual activity at all.
Someone vowed to virginity (usually a woman and often a consecrated virgin), or someone who died in defense of their virginity; (especially) one venerated as a saint.
ex: In its list of saints, the Catholic Church classifies St. Agnes, St. Maria Goretti, and St. Thérèse of Lisieux as virgins.

senses.d: One who has never used or experienced a specified thing.
ex: I've never eaten tofu before—you could say I'm a tofu virgin.

senses.d: Any of several species of gossamer-winged butterflies of the family Lycaenidae.
A female insect producing eggs from which young are hatched, though there has been no fecundation by a male; a parthenogenetic insect.
In a state of virginity; chaste, not having had sexual intercourse.
ex: Innocence and virgin Modestie […] / That would be woo’d, and not unsought be won

senses.d: Of a physical object, untouched.
ex: The white cold virgin snow upon my heart / Abates the ardour of my liver.

senses.d: Not yet cultivated, explored, or exploited by humans or humans of certain civilizations.
ex: virgin prairie
virgin ecosystem

senses.d: Inexperienced.
ex: The woman shook dangerously, an obvious virgin gunhandler.

senses.d: Of olive oil, obtained by mechanical means, so that the oil is not altered.
ex: Wondering how some oil is somehow more virgin than regular virgin olive oil can be a real head-scratcher.

senses.d: Of mixed drinks, not containing alcohol.
ex: a virgin daiquiri
